claim: Trp2 is an enzyme involved in melanin biosynthesis encoded by the dopachrome tautomerase (Dct) gene.
source: Trp2, an enzyme involved in melanin biosynthesis encoded by the dopachrome tautomerase (Dct) gene, is normally expressed by melanocytes in the skin in both humans and C57BL/6 mice and is overexpressed by many melanomas (Avogadri et al., 2016; Wang et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Avogadri et al., 2016; Wang et al., 1996).

claim: Trp2 is normally expressed by melanocytes in the skin in both humans and C57BL/6 mice.
source: Trp2, an enzyme involved in melanin biosynthesis encoded by the dopachrome tautomerase (Dct) gene, is normally expressed by melanocytes in the skin in both humans and C57BL/6 mice and is overexpressed by many melanomas (Avogadri et al., 2016; Wang et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Avogadri et al., 2016; Wang et al., 1996).

claim: Trp2 is overexpressed by many melanomas.
source: Trp2, an enzyme involved in melanin biosynthesis encoded by the dopachrome tautomerase (Dct) gene, is normally expressed by melanocytes in the skin in both humans and C57BL/6 mice and is overexpressed by many melanomas (Avogadri et al., 2016; Wang et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Avogadri et al., 2016; Wang et al., 1996).

claim: Thymic clonal deletion is less effective than previously thought.
source: However, recent studies have revealed that thymic clonal deletion is less effective than previously thought (Richards et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Richards et al., 2016).

claim: Self-reactive CD8+ T cells have been shown to escape negative selection in mice.
source: Self-reactive CD8+ T cells have been shown to escape negative selection in mice (Bouneaud et al., 2000; Zehn and Bevan, 2006), with one group proposing that up to 4% of peripheral CD8+ T cells are self-specific (Richards et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Bouneaud et al., 2000; Zehn and Bevan, 2006).

claim: Up to 4% of peripheral CD8+ T cells are self-specific.
source: Self-reactive CD8+ T cells have been shown to escape negative selection in mice (Bouneaud et al., 2000; Zehn and Bevan, 2006), with one group proposing that up to 4% of peripheral CD8+ T cells are self-specific (Richards et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Richards et al., 2015).

claim: Precursor frequencies of blood CD8+ T cells specific for certain self-peptides were comparable to those demonstrated for foreign peptides in humans.
source: Furthermore, studies in humans indicated that precursor frequencies of blood CD8+ T cells specific for certain self-peptides were comparable to those demonstrated for foreign peptides (Yu et al., 2015) and suggested that such cells might be capable of overt autoreactivity if suitably stimulated (Maeda et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Yu et al., 2015).

claim: Self-specific CD8+ T cells might be capable of overt autoreactivity if suitably stimulated.
source: Furthermore, studies in humans indicated that precursor frequencies of blood CD8+ T cells specific for certain self-peptides were comparable to those demonstrated for foreign peptides (Yu et al., 2015) and suggested that such cells might be capable of overt autoreactivity if suitably stimulated (Maeda et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Maeda et al., 2014).

claim: The Dct-deficient strain carries a large deletion encompassing exon 2 encoding Trp2180–188.
source: For mice in which Trp2 would not be a self-antigen, we used a novel Dct-/- strain that carries a large deletion encompassing the exon (exon 2) encoding Trp2180–188 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 1—source data 2 and 3), unlike a previously described Dct-targeted strain that retains the coding sequence for that epitope (Guyonneau et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and source data, and by citation to published literature (Guyonneau et al., 2004).

claim: More than 1500 Trp2/Kb-specific CD8+ T cells were identified in both WT and Dct-/- mice.
source: While on average we identified more antigen-specific cells in Dct-/- mice (~1.4-fold increased), we nevertheless found relatively large numbers of Trp2/Kb-specific CD8+ T cells (>1500) in both strains, evidence that most Trp2/Kb-specific cells escape thymic or peripheral clonal deletion in WT mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from tetramer enrichment experiments.

claim: Most Trp2/Kb-specific cells escape thymic or peripheral clonal deletion in WT mice.
source: While on average we identified more antigen-specific cells in Dct-/- mice (~1.4-fold increased), we nevertheless found relatively large numbers of Trp2/Kb-specific CD8+ T cells (>1500) in both strains, evidence that most Trp2/Kb-specific cells escape thymic or peripheral clonal deletion in WT mice.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing large numbers of Trp2/Kb-specific cells in WT mice.

claim: Dct-/- mice have approximately 1.4-fold more Trp2/Kb-specific CD8+ T cells than WT mice.
source: While on average we identified more antigen-specific cells in Dct-/- mice (~1.4-fold increased), we nevertheless found relatively large numbers of Trp2/Kb-specific CD8+ T cells (>1500) in both strains, evidence that most Trp2/Kb-specific cells escape thymic or peripheral clonal deletion in WT mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from tetramer enrichment experiments.

claim: The average Trp2/Kb tetramer staining was higher on Dct-/- cells compared to WT cells.
source: The average Trp2/Kb tetramer staining was higher on Dct-/- cells, but the MFI largely overlapped between the two populations (Figure 1B), suggesting that the range of TCR avidities did not markedly differ between the Trp2/Kb-specific pools.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The range of TCR avidities did not markedly differ between the Trp2/Kb-specific pools in WT and Dct-/- mice.
source: The average Trp2/Kb tetramer staining was higher on Dct-/- cells, but the MFI largely overlapped between the two populations (Figure 1B), suggesting that the range of TCR avidities did not markedly differ between the Trp2/Kb-specific pools.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the overlapping MFI data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The WT:Dct-/- tetramer MFI ratio is approximately 0.8.
source: While analysis of unimmunized mice revealed that the average number and tetramer staining intensity of Trp2/Kb-specific CD8+ T cells were significantly lower in WT than Dct-/- animals, the degree of overlap suggests such measures would be unreliable for detecting tolerant cells beyond this optimized experimental model. Furthermore, the relatively consistent WT to Dct-/- tetramer MFI ratio in our time course experiments argues against an imbalanced outgrowth of higher affinity/avidity TCR clones in Dct-/- relative to WT animals (as might have been expected if TCR affinity was the primary factor driving improved proliferation in the Dct-/- population).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from tetramer staining experiments.

claim: The tetramer MFI of B8R/Kb-specific cells was comparable between WT and Dct-/- strains.
source: As a control to make sure there were no staining differences between the strains, we also assessed the avidity of cells specific for an irrelevant foreign epitope—B8R/Kb from vaccinia virus—in WT and Dct-/- mice; the tetramer MFI of B8R/Kb-specific cells was comparable between the strains as expected (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: No consistent differences in the expression of activation/memory markers (CD69, CD44, CD122) were identified between Dct-/- and WT Trp2/Kb-specific cells in pre-immune mice.
source: We also examined the phenotype of Trp2/Kb-specific cells in pre-immune WT and Dct-/- mice. No consistent differences in the expression of activation/memory markers (CD69, CD44, CD122) or anergy/exhaustion markers (PD-1, LAG3, CTLA-4, TIM3) were identified between Dct-/- and WT Trp2/Kb-specific cells (Figure 1D–F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1D-F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B-D.

claim: No consistent differences in the expression of anergy/exhaustion markers (PD-1, LAG3, CTLA-4, TIM3) were identified between Dct-/- and WT Trp2/Kb-specific cells in pre-immune mice.
source: We also examined the phenotype of Trp2/Kb-specific cells in pre-immune WT and Dct-/- mice. No consistent differences in the expression of activation/memory markers (CD69, CD44, CD122) or anergy/exhaustion markers (PD-1, LAG3, CTLA-4, TIM3) were identified between Dct-/- and WT Trp2/Kb-specific cells (Figure 1D–F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1D-F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B-D.

claim: The majority of Trp2/Kb-specific cells exhibited low expression of the memory markers CD44 and CD122 in pre-immune mice.
source: The majority of cells exhibited low expression of the memory markers CD44 and CD122, and anergy/exhaustion marker expression was low in both populations.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from flow cytometry analysis.

claim: Anergy/exhaustion marker expression was low in both WT and Dct-/- Trp2/Kb-specific cell populations in pre-immune mice.
source: The majority of cells exhibited low expression of the memory markers CD44 and CD122, and anergy/exhaustion marker expression was low in both populations.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from flow cytometry analysis.

claim: No significant differences in CD5 expression were detected between WT and Dct-/- Trp2/Kb-specific cells in pre-immune mice.
source: CD5 can indicate self-antigen recognition (Azzam et al., 1998; Fulton et al., 2015), but we did not detect significant differences in expression between the groups (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G and citations to published literature (Azzam et al., 1998; Fulton et al., 2015).

claim: RNAseq analysis of Trp2/Kb tetramer-binding cells isolated from pre-immune mice showed no consistent differences in gene expression between WT and Dct-/- mice.
source: RNAseq analysis of Trp2/Kb tetramer-binding cells isolated from pre-immune mice by fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) showed no consistent differences in gene expression related to their derivation from WT versus Dct-/- mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E), although this does not rule out the possibility of epigenetic differences between the populations.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: CD8+ T cells specific for Trp2363/Db and Trp1455/Db are present at similar or slightly lower numbers in mice expressing antigen relative to mutant mice.
source: To ensure our findings were not unique to Trp2180/Kb-specific cells, we used tetramer enrichment to isolate CD8+ T cells specific for other skin antigens—a distinct Trp2 epitope (Trp2363/Db) and a tyrosinase-related protein 1 epitope (Trp1455/Db)—in mice expressing or lacking these antigens. We were able to identify cells with these specificities present at numbers similar to slightly less in mice expressing antigen relative to mutant mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F.

claim: CD8+ T cells specific for other melanocyte self-epitopes also largely escape clonal deletion.
source: This suggests that CD8+ T cells specific for other melanocyte self-epitopes also largely escape clonal deletion.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing similar numbers of cells specific for other melanocyte epitopes in antigen-expressing and mutant mice.

claim: WT mice showed a more limited response to Trp2 at day 7 after TriVax relative to Dct-/- mice.
source: While WT and Dct-/- mice responded similarly to B8R, WT mice showed a more limited response to Trp2 at an effector time point (day 7) relative to Dct-/- mice (Figure 2A,B), ruling out this type of ignorance as the dominant tolerance mechanism.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: WT and Dct-/- mice responded similarly to B8R peptide after TriVax immunization.
source: While WT and Dct-/- mice responded similarly to B8R, WT mice showed a more limited response to Trp2 at an effector time point (day 7) relative to Dct-/- mice (Figure 2A,B), ruling out this type of ignorance as the dominant tolerance mechanism.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: A significantly larger number and frequency of Trp2/Kb-specific cells were observed in Dct-/- mice at day 7 after TriVax.
source: We observed a significantly larger number and frequency of Trp2/Kb-specific cells in Dct-/- mice, and the Dct-/- cells exhibited higher apparent Trp2/Kb avidity (as measured by tetramer MFI; Figure 2C–E); TCRß MFI was similar between WT and Dct-/- Trp2/Kb-specific cells, indicating that the difference in tetramer MFI between the strains did not reflect differential modulation of cell-surface TCR (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2C-E.

claim: Dct-/- Trp2/Kb-specific cells exhibited higher apparent Trp2/Kb avidity at day 7 after TriVax.
source: We observed a significantly larger number and frequency of Trp2/Kb-specific cells in Dct-/- mice, and the Dct-/- cells exhibited higher apparent Trp2/Kb avidity (as measured by tetramer MFI; Figure 2C–E); TCRß MFI was similar between WT and Dct-/- Trp2/Kb-specific cells, indicating that the difference in tetramer MFI between the strains did not reflect differential modulation of cell-surface TCR (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2C-E.

claim: TCRß MFI was similar between WT and Dct-/- Trp2/Kb-specific cells at day 7 after TriVax.
source: We observed a significantly larger number and frequency of Trp2/Kb-specific cells in Dct-/- mice, and the Dct-/- cells exhibited higher apparent Trp2/Kb avidity (as measured by tetramer MFI; Figure 2C–E); TCRß MFI was similar between WT and Dct-/- Trp2/Kb-specific cells, indicating that the difference in tetramer MFI between the strains did not reflect differential modulation of cell-surface TCR (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: WT Trp2/Kb-specific cells expanded more than 1000-fold after TriVax immunization.
source: Still, WT Trp2/Kb-specific cells expanded >1000-fold (Dct-/- cells expanded ~4000-fold).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from tetramer enumeration experiments.

claim: Dct-/- Trp2/Kb-specific cells expanded approximately 4000-fold after TriVax immunization.
source: Still, WT Trp2/Kb-specific cells expanded >1000-fold (Dct-/- cells expanded ~4000-fold).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from tetramer enumeration experiments.

claim: The frequency of PD-1+ cells was comparable between WT and Dct-/- Trp2/Kb-specific populations at day 7 after TriVax.
source: The frequency of PD-1+ cells was comparable between WT and Dct-/- Trp2/Kb-specific populations (Figure 2F), suggesting similar exposure to antigen.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: A greater frequency of Dct-/- CD8+ T cells produced IFN-γ, TNF-α, and CD107a at day 7 after TriVax following ex vivo Trp2 stimulation.
source: We also assessed cytokine production and degranulation following ex vivo Trp2 stimulation at day 7 after TriVax and found that a greater frequency of Dct-/- CD8+ T cells produced IFN-γ, TNF-α, and CD107a (an indicator of degranulation), in approximate proportion to the frequency of Trp2/Kb-specific cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: A slightly larger proportion of Dct-/- IFN-γ-producing cells co-produced TNF-α at day 7 after TriVax.
source: Among IFN-γ-producing cells, a slightly larger proportion of Dct-/- cells co-produced TNF-α, indicating that Trp2/Kb-specific Dct-/- cells may have modestly improved polyfunctionality (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The number of Trp2/Kb-specific cells in the skin was similar between WT and Dct-/- strains at day 7 after TriVax.
source: Interestingly, this was not the case: the number of Trp2/Kb-specific cells in the skin was similar between the strains (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The Trp2/Kb-specific response was greater in Dct-/- mice at both effector (day 7) and memory (day 45) time points after LmTrp2 infection.
source: Again, the Trp2/Kb-specific response was greater in Dct-/- mice at both effector and memory time points (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A-C.

claim: Transferred WT Trp2/Kb-specific cells expanded approximately 100-fold after TriVax boost.
source: Transferred WT Trp2/Kb-specific cells did proliferate (~100-fold expansion), albeit to a much lesser degree than endogenous Dct-/- Trp2/Kb-specific cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from adoptive transfer experiments.

claim: Transferred WT Trp2/Kb-specific cells showed comparable expansion in both WT and Dct-/- recipients after TriVax boost.
source: Importantly, their expansion was comparable in both WT and Dct-/- recipients (Figure 3B,D), suggesting that the WT CD8+ T cells remained hyporesponsive even in an environment where endogenous cells were not tolerant to Trp2, supporting a cell-intrinsic basis for the impaired reactivity of WT Trp2/Kb-specific CD8+ T cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3B and 3D.

claim: The impaired reactivity of WT Trp2/Kb-specific CD8+ T cells has a cell-intrinsic basis.
source: Importantly, their expansion was comparable in both WT and Dct-/- recipients (Figure 3B,D), suggesting that the WT CD8+ T cells remained hyporesponsive even in an environment where endogenous cells were not tolerant to Trp2, supporting a cell-intrinsic basis for the impaired reactivity of WT Trp2/Kb-specific CD8+ T cells.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing similar expansion of transferred WT cells in both WT and Dct-/- recipients.

claim: Transferred Dct-/- Trp2/Kb-specific cells expanded robustly in both Dct-/- and WT recipients after TriVax boost.
source: These Trp2/Kb-specific donor cells were able to expand robustly in both Dct-/- and WT recipients (Figure 3C,E), further demonstrating a lack of extrinsic regulation in the WT environment.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3C and 3E.

claim: There is a lack of extrinsic regulation in the WT environment that would limit Trp2/Kb-specific cell responses.
source: These Trp2/Kb-specific donor cells were able to expand robustly in both Dct-/- and WT recipients (Figure 3C,E), further demonstrating a lack of extrinsic regulation in the WT environment.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing robust expansion of transferred Dct-/- cells in WT recipients.

claim: Dct-/- cells performed better in WT recipients than in Dct-/- recipients after TriVax boost.
source: Dct-/- cells actually performed better in WT recipients than in Dct-/- recipients; the basis for this outcome is not clear but could be due to reduced competition by endogenous Trp2/Kb-specific cells in WT hosts.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from adoptive transfer experiments.

claim: Cell-intrinsic mechanisms enforce tolerance among WT Trp2/Kb-specific cells.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that cell-intrinsic mechanism(s) enforce tolerance among WT Trp2/Kb-specific cells.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data from adoptive transfer experiments.

claim: WT Trp2/Kb-specific cells were capable of an initial response that largely paralleled that shown by their Dct-/- counterparts after TriVax immunization.
source: Interestingly, WT Trp2/Kb-specific cells were capable of an initial response that largely paralleled that shown by their Dct-/- counterparts (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: By days 6 and 7 after high-dose TriVax immunization, Trp2/Kb-specific cells in Dct-/- mice outnumbered those in WT mice by an average ratio of 4:1.
source: By days 6 and 7 after high-dose TriVax immunization, Trp2/Kb-specific cells in Dct-/- mice outnumbered those in WT mice by an average ratio of 4:1.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from time course experiments.

claim: The proportion of Trp2/Kb-specific cells expressing CD25 was significantly greater in Dct-/- mice on day 4 after TriVax.
source: The proportion of Trp2/Kb-specific cells expressing CD25 was significantly greater in Dct-/- mice on day 4, and trended higher on days 2 and 3 (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4B and 4C.

claim: The CD25 MFI of CD25+ cells was higher on Dct-/- Trp2/Kb-specific cells on day 4 after TriVax.
source: The CD25 MFI of CD25+ cells was also higher on Dct-/- Trp2/Kb-specific cells on day 4 (Figure 4B and C), suggesting that Dct-/- cells expressed more CD25 on a per-cell basis.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4B and 4C.

claim: Dct-/- Trp2/Kb-specific cells displayed significantly higher tetramer MFI than WT cells on days 2 through 7 after TriVax.
source: Once again, Dct-/- Trp2/Kb-specific cells displayed significantly higher tetramer MFI than WT cells on days 2 through 7, but the avidity differences detected by tetramer staining did not demonstrate a progressive increase with time; the ratio between the WT and Dct-/- tetramer MFI transiently dropped at days 4–6, but the ratio at day 7 was similar to that of pre-immune cells (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The response to Trp2/Kb in WT and Dct-/- mice follows similar kinetics and magnitude but expansion in WT animals terminates prematurely.
source: These findings indicate that the response to Trp2/Kb in WT and Dct-/- mice follows similar kinetics and magnitude but that expansion in WT animals terminates prematurely.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data from time course experiments.

claim: The distribution of WT and Dct-/- Trp2/Kb-specific cells was quite similar at day 7 after TriVax based on single-cell RNA sequencing.
source: Surprisingly, the distribution of WT and Dct-/- cells was quite similar (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A); the majority of clusters showed similar frequencies of cells from the two strains, although a slightly larger proportion of Dct-/- cells (14% versus 6% of WT cells) were located in cluster 1 and a slightly smaller proportion in cluster 2 (5% versus 12% of WT cells).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Over half of the cells (58%) from Dct-/- mice were localized in cluster 0 at day 3 after TriVax.
source: Interestingly, over half of the cells (58%) from Dct-/- mice were localized in cluster 0, but this cluster was nearly devoid of WT cells, representing only a small subset (13%) of WT cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Cluster 0 represented only a small subset (13%) of WT cells at day 3 after TriVax.
source: Interestingly, over half of the cells (58%) from Dct-/- mice were localized in cluster 0, but this cluster was nearly devoid of WT cells, representing only a small subset (13%) of WT cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Histone genes were among the most upregulated in Group A compared to Group B at day 3 after TriVax.
source: Histone genes (e.g., Hist1h1b, Hist1h1e, Hist1h1d, Hist2h2ac) were among the most upregulated in Group A compared to Group B; these genes are commonly induced in association with cellular replication (Mei et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and citation to published literature (Mei et al., 2017).

claim: Other genes associated with proliferation, such as Myc, Nolc1, Npm1, and Ccne2, were upregulated in Group A at day 3 after TriVax.
source: Other genes associated with proliferation, such as Myc, Nolc1, Npm1, and Ccne2, were also upregulated in Group A (Figure 5C), and cell cycle analysis revealed that the majority of cells in Group A were in stages G2/M or S of the cell cycle (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The majority of cells in Group A were in stages G2/M or S of the cell cycle at day 3 after TriVax.
source: Other genes associated with proliferation, such as Myc, Nolc1, Npm1, and Ccne2, were also upregulated in Group A (Figure 5C), and cell cycle analysis revealed that the majority of cells in Group A were in stages G2/M or S of the cell cycle (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Among cells in cluster 0, 76% of Dct-/- cells were in G2/M or S versus 42% of WT cells at day 3 after TriVax.
source: Among cells in cluster 0 (Group A), 76% of Dct-/- cells were in G2/M or S versus 42% of WT cells (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Gene set enrichment analysis revealed a strong enrichment of gene sets comprising Myc targets, E2F targets, and genes related to mTORC1 signaling and the G2/M checkpoint in Group A at day 3 after TriVax.
source: Gene set enrichment analysis revealed a strong enrichment of gene sets comprising Myc targets, E2F targets, and genes related to mTORC1 signaling and the G2/M checkpoint (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Many of the cells in Group A expressed CD25 at day 3 after TriVax.
source: Many of the cells in Group A expressed CD25, with the majority of the remainder located in cluster 2 of Group B (Figure 5F); cells in these clusters also showed enrichment for a gene signature associated with IL-2 receptor signaling (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Group A cells showed significantly higher expression of Irf4 and Myc at day 3 after TriVax.
source: Indeed, Group A cells showed significantly higher expression of certain genes relevant to the IL-2 signaling pathway with known impacts on T cell function, such as Irf4 and Myc; previous work has demonstrated that signaling through the IL-2 receptor is important for sustained Myc expression (Preston et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from single-cell RNA sequencing and citation to published literature (Preston et al., 2015).

claim: IL-2 complex treatment on day 5 after TriVax or LmTrp2 improved the expansion of both WT and Dct-/- Trp2/Kb-specific cells to a similar extent.
source: IL-2 complex treatment on day 5 after TriVax or LmTrp2 improved the expansion of both WT and Dct-/- Trp2/Kb-specific cells to a similar extent (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D,E.

claim: WT Trp2/Kb-specific cells are deficient in their ability to form the more proliferative subpopulation that comprises a majority of the Dct-/- Trp2/Kb-specific population on day 3 after priming.
source: Taken as a whole, the RNA-sequencing data suggest that WT Trp2/Kb-specific cells are deficient in their ability to form the more proliferative subpopulation that comprises a majority of the Dct-/- Trp2/Kb-specific population on day 3 after priming.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the single-cell RNA sequencing data.

claim: Recipients of Dct-/- cells developed vitiligo more rapidly and more extensively than mice receiving WT cells.
source: Recipients of Dct-/- cells developed vitiligo more rapidly and more extensively than mice receiving WT cells, beginning around day 20 after cell transfer (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Vitiligo progressed more rapidly and to a greater extent in recipients of Dct-/- cells compared to recipients of WT cells.
source: Vitiligo progressed more rapidly and to a greater extent (higher numeric score) in recipients of Dct-/- cells (Figure 6D; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C), although low-grade vitiligo was observed in some mice receiving WT Trp2/Kb-specific effector cells or TriVax and DNFB without cell transfer.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Vitiligo severity was positively correlated with the number of donor Trp2/Kb-specific cells in the blood on day 6 after transfer and TriVax boost.
source: Vitiligo severity (average vitiligo score) was positively correlated with the number of donor Trp2/Kb-specific cells in the blood on day 6 after transfer and TriVax boost (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Similar numbers of transferred Trp2/Kb-specific cells from both WT and Dct-/- donors were identified in the DNFB-treated flank at day 11 or 12 after cell transfer.
source: At day 11 or 12 after cell transfer, we identified similar numbers of cells from both donors in the DNFB-treated (left) flank; interestingly, this number was also similar to the number of cells identified in the vehicle-treated (right) flank (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The phenotype (PD-1, CD49a expression) of the transferred Trp2/Kb-specific cells was similar across donor group and both flanks at day 11 or 12 after cell transfer.
source: The phenotype (PD-1, CD49a expression) of the transferred Trp2/Kb-specific cells was also similar across donor group and both flanks (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Differences in skin recruitment and retention are unlikely to account for the distinct disease progression induced by WT and Dct-/- Trp2/Kb-specific cell populations.
source: These findings contrasted with the clear difference in vitiligo elicited by Dct-/- versus WT cells and indicate that differences in skin recruitment and retention are unlikely to account for the distinct disease progression induced by these populations.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing similar numbers and phenotypes of transferred cells in the skin despite different vitiligo outcomes.

claim: The ability of WT and Dct-/- Trp2/Kb-specific cell populations to mediate autoimmune damage was strikingly different.
source: In summary, in contrast to the relatively modest differences in the expansion of Trp2/Kb responders in WT and Dct-/- mice, the ability of these populations to mediate autoimmune damage—melanocyte destruction—was strikingly different.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data comparing expansion and vitiligo induction.

claim: Tolerance among Trp2/Kb-specific CD8+ T cells is manifest primarily at the level of minimizing overt autoimmunity.
source: Here, we show that tolerance among Trp2/Kb-specific CD8+ T cells is manifest primarily at the level of minimizing overt autoimmunity; differences in the size and initial Trp2 responsiveness of the precursor pool in WT and Dct-/- mice were relatively modest, although there was evidence for 'pruning' of cells with the highest avidity Trp2/Kb-specific TCRs from the WT precursor population.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing modest differences in precursor frequency and responsiveness but striking differences in vitiligo induction.

claim: There was evidence for 'pruning' of cells with the highest avidity Trp2/Kb-specific TCRs from the WT precursor population.
source: Here, we show that tolerance among Trp2/Kb-specific CD8+ T cells is manifest primarily at the level of minimizing overt autoimmunity; differences in the size and initial Trp2 responsiveness of the precursor pool in WT and Dct-/- mice were relatively modest, although there was evidence for 'pruning' of cells with the highest avidity Trp2/Kb-specific TCRs from the WT precursor population.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing higher tetramer MFI in Dct-/- cells.

claim: The underlying tolerance mechanism does not depend on cell-extrinsic regulation but correlates with a cell-intrinsic failure of WT Trp2/Kb-specific CD8+ T cells to sustain optimal proliferation.
source: The underlying tolerance mechanism does not depend on cell-extrinsic regulation but rather correlates with a cell-intrinsic failure of WT Trp2/Kb-specific CD8+ T cells to sustain optimal proliferation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data from adoptive transfer experiments and proliferation assays.

claim: Reduced CD25 expression and impaired differentiation into a highly proliferative subpopulation correlate with functional tolerance of a T cell population.
source: Moreover, our polyclonal model reveals that certain characteristics of Trp2/Kb-responsive effector cells—reduced CD25 expression and impaired differentiation into a highly proliferative subpopulation—correlate with functional tolerance of a T cell population, providing a framework for future characterization of self-specific CD8+ T cells.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing reduced CD25 expression and impaired proliferation in WT cells.

claim: Trp2 is a common target in cancer immunotherapy directed against melanoma.
source: This model is relevant to human health, as Trp2 is a common target in cancer immunotherapy directed against melanoma (Cho and Celis, 2009; Liu et al., 2014; Parkhurst et al., 1998), and Trp2/Kb-specific responses can be induced in WT mice with vigorous priming approaches (Bowne et al., 1999; Byrne et al., 2011; Cho and Celis, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Cho and Celis, 2009; Liu et al., 2014; Parkhurst et al., 1998).

claim: Trp2/Kb-specific responses can be induced in WT mice with vigorous priming approaches.
source: This model is relevant to human health, as Trp2 is a common target in cancer immunotherapy directed against melanoma (Cho and Celis, 2009; Liu et al., 2014; Parkhurst et al., 1998), and Trp2/Kb-specific responses can be induced in WT mice with vigorous priming approaches (Bowne et al., 1999; Byrne et al., 2011; Cho and Celis, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Bowne et al., 1999; Byrne et al., 2011; Cho and Celis, 2009).

claim: Tolerance in this setting does not lead to marked changes in the presence, phenotype, or initial reactivity of Trp2/Kb-specific CD8+ T cells but limits these cells' capacity for overt autoreactivity.
source: Accordingly, we conclude that tolerance in this setting does not lead to marked changes in the presence, phenotype, or initial reactivity of Trp2/Kb-specific CD8+ T cells but limits these cells' capacity for overt autoreactivity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing similar precursor frequencies and phenotypes but different vitiligo induction.

claim: Self-reactive cells are often reported to express inhibitory receptors such as CTLA-4, PD-1, and LAG-3.
source: In some cases, self-reactive cells display indicators of reduced functionality, revealing them as tolerant and unlikely to cause spontaneous pathology. For example, self-reactive cells are often reported to express inhibitory receptors such as CTLA-4, PD-1, and LAG-3 (Fife and Bluestone, 2008; Maeda et al., 2014; Nelson et al., 2019; Schietinger et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Fife and Bluestone, 2008; Maeda et al., 2014; Nelson et al., 2019; Schietinger et al., 2012).

claim: Studies in human adults have identified self-reactive cells with a phenotype similar to that of naïve CD8+ T cells specific for foreign antigens.
source: However, studies in human adults have identified self-reactive cells with a phenotype similar to that of naïve CD8+ T cells specific for foreign antigens (Yu et al., 2015); these cells did not display an overtly anergic phenotype but still responded poorly to stimulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Yu et al., 2015).

claim: The 'pruning' of WT CD8+ T cells with high-avidity Trp2/Kb-specific TCRs appears to be remarkably subtle.
source: The 'pruning' of WT CD8+ T cells with high-avidity Trp2/Kb-specific TCRs remains the most likely explanation for this finding. If so, however, the effect of such pruning appears to be remarkably subtle.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing modest differences in tetramer MFI.

claim: The relatively modest differences in cell number and tetramer staining between tolerant and non-tolerant cells would not be sufficient to accurately predict self-reactivity versus tolerance in a clinical setting.
source: At a practical level, the relatively modest differences in cell number and tetramer staining between tolerant and non-tolerant cells that we observed in this carefully controlled model system would not be sufficient to accurately predict self-reactivity versus tolerance in a clinical setting.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing overlapping precursor frequencies and tetramer MFI.

claim: Even CD8+ T cells with very-low-affinity/avidity TCRs can provoke overt tissue damage that may reach or exceed the response observed for non-tolerant, high-affinity/avidity cells.
source: Other studies utilizing mouse models have reported that even CD8+ T cells with very-low-affinity/avidity TCRs (including those undetectable by normal peptide/MHC tetramer staining) can provoke overt tissue damage that may reach or exceed the response observed for non-tolerant, high-affinity/avidity cells (Enouz et al., 2012; Sabatino et al., 2011; Zehn and Bevan, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Enouz et al., 2012; Sabatino et al., 2011; Zehn and Bevan, 2006).

claim: The impact of CD8+ T cell tolerance toward some self-antigens only partially limits expansion but can prevent the generation of cells readily capable of potent tissue destruction.
source: Hence, the impact of CD8+ T cell tolerance toward some self-antigens only partially limits expansion but can prevent the generation of cells readily capable of potent tissue destruction: tolerance is not a binary state.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing modest differences in expansion but striking differences in vitiligo induction.

claim: Tolerance is not a binary state.
source: Hence, the impact of CD8+ T cell tolerance toward some self-antigens only partially limits expansion but can prevent the generation of cells readily capable of potent tissue destruction: tolerance is not a binary state.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing a spectrum of tolerance effects.

claim: WT responders failed to differentiate into a CD25+, IRF4+ population soon after priming.
source: Flow cytometry and single-cell RNA sequencing of Trp2/Kb-specific CD8+ T cells soon after priming demonstrated that WT responders failed to differentiate into a CD25+, IRF4+ population (a characteristic of most Dct-/- responder cells) and indicated that WT cells showed poor commitment to sustained proliferation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from flow cytometry and single-cell RNA sequencing.

claim: WT cells showed poor commitment to sustained proliferation soon after priming.
source: Flow cytometry and single-cell RNA sequencing of Trp2/Kb-specific CD8+ T cells soon after priming demonstrated that WT responders failed to differentiate into a CD25+, IRF4+ population (a characteristic of most Dct-/- responder cells) and indicated that WT cells showed poor commitment to sustained proliferation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from flow cytometry and single-cell RNA sequencing.

claim: The early effector population of Trp2/Kb-specific cells demonstrates heterogeneity on a transcriptomic level in both strains.
source: The early effector population of Trp2/Kb-specific cells demonstrates heterogeneity on a transcriptomic level in both strains.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from single-cell RNA sequencing.

claim: The majority of Dct-/- cells show a highly proliferative phenotype characterized by active cell cycling and responsiveness to mTOR and Myc.
source: Whereas the majority of Dct-/- cells show a highly proliferative phenotype characterized by active cell cycling and responsiveness to mTOR and Myc, few WT Trp2/Kb-specific cells fall into this group.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from single-cell RNA sequencing.

claim: Few WT Trp2/Kb-specific cells show a highly proliferative phenotype characterized by active cell cycling and responsiveness to mTOR and Myc.
source: Whereas the majority of Dct-/- cells show a highly proliferative phenotype characterized by active cell cycling and responsiveness to mTOR and Myc, few WT Trp2/Kb-specific cells fall into this group.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from single-cell RNA sequencing.

claim: Epigenetic changes in chromatin accessibility or methylation can maintain dysfunctional or exhausted states in CD8+ T cells.
source: Recent studies on dysfunctional tumor-specific or exhausted CD8+ T cells have shown that epigenetic changes in chromatin accessibility or methylation can maintain such states (Ghoneim et al., 2017; Pauken et al., 2016; Philip et al., 2017), which is one potential explanation for the cell-intrinsic nature of the tolerance seen in our model.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Ghoneim et al., 2017; Pauken et al., 2016; Philip et al., 2017).

claim: The ability of self-specific cells to respond to self-antigen immunization while not causing autoimmune damage is relevant for understanding the limits of 'breaking' tolerance for cancer immunotherapy.
source: Accordingly, we predict that our results will apply to other populations of CD8+ T cells specific for melanocyte and potentially other tissue-restricted antigens. Similar populations of self-specific CD8+ T cells may exist in humans, and the ability of such cells to respond to self-antigen immunization while not causing autoimmune damage is relevant for understanding the limits of 'breaking' tolerance, for example, for cancer immunotherapy.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data and speculation about clinical relevance.

claim: Results from this study align with work examining polyclonal self-antigen-specific cells in human adults with regard to phenotype and response to cognate peptide.
source: Indeed, our results align with work examining polyclonal self-antigen-specific cells in human adults (Yu et al., 2015) with regard to the phenotype (modestly lower tetramer MFI, lower CD25 expression) and response to cognate peptide (diminished) observed among tolerant cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to published literature (Yu et al., 2015).

claim: This model has clear relevance to human physiology.
source: This model has clear relevance to human physiology and will be useful in exploring methods of correcting the proliferative defects of tolerant cells to more effectively mobilize them in cancer immunotherapy approaches targeting tumor antigens shared with self.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data and speculation about clinical relevance.
